Filter by hard constraints such as dates, party size, location, and availability before learning-to-rank. Retrieve feasible listings, then rank using relevance, price/value, booking propensity, and probability that the stay completes without host cancellation. A lower cancellation rate should affect expected utility, not masquerade as a relevance signal.

Model the session’s comparison process across many listings and visits. Attribution windows and repeated browsing matter: an unbooked impression is not necessarily a strong negative, and delayed booking labels require maturity. Features must reflect price and availability as seen at the time, not today’s values. Include cold-start content features for new listings.

Use diversity and geographic coverage to support comparison rather than filling the page with near duplicates. Evaluate completed bookings, cancellations, customer service incidents, search effort, and host exposure. Marketplace effects can make ordinary user-randomized tests difficult; consider appropriate geographic/time experiments. Serve a deterministic feasibility-aware fallback if personalization is unavailable.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** A simple expected completed-booking quantity is $P(book|x)[1-P(cancel|book,x)]$, but utility also includes relevance, experience, and marketplace constraints. Calibrate the component probabilities on mature outcomes. Feasibility filters must reflect current inventory, while training features must reflect historical inventory at the prediction time; mixing those snapshots creates leakage.
